strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in AI for chemistry: while many prior works assess LLMs via high-level property prediction or ambiguous text descriptions, MolLangBench rigorously targets fundamental, deterministic, structure-grounded molecular recognition, editing, and generation.

Exceptionally rigorous annotation and multi-stage verification pipeline for editing and generation tasks, requiring independent chemical redrawings by domain experts to ensure that prompts are completely unambiguous and lead to a single unique ground truth.

Extensive benchmarking across state-of-the-art frontier models, including reasoning-focused models (o1, o3, o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-5), standard LLMs, vision-language models, and open-source chemistry-specific LLMs.

Deep and insightful error analysis, particularly pinpointing the atom localization drop caused by standard byte-pair encoding (BPE) tokenization merging multiple atoms into single tokens, as well as highlighting the acute failure modes in stereochemical reasoning (E/Z and R/S configuration).
Thorough supplementary evaluations, including prompt robustness/sensitivity analyses, run-to-run variance quantification, and OCR-assisted evaluation pipelines for visual generation.
weaknesses: The dataset size for editing and generation is relatively small (200 core instances and 200 extended instances each), which, while justifiable given the high human annotation cost (30-60 minutes per instance), limits fine-grained stratification across diverse chemical scaffolds.
Although the paper notes that the benchmark formulation conceptually supports molecular graphs, practical graph-language models are omitted from the empirical evaluation.

Evaluating tool-integrated or agentic baselines (e.g., LLMs equipped with standard cheminformatics toolkits like RDKit or code execution) would provide a stronger benchmark context, as practical chemical workflows frequently leverage tool use rather than pure zero-shot string completion.

strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing a critical gap: unlike existing chemistry-language datasets that mix functional/pharmacological metadata with ambiguous structural descriptions, MolLangBench emphasizes deterministic, unambiguous, and structure-grounded tasks (recognition, editing, and generation).

Rigorous data curation and validation methodology: the three-stage human annotation protocol for editing and generation (initial authoring, peer review, and dual independent blind reconstruction by chemistry experts) guarantees high fidelity and uniquely resolvable ground-truth molecules.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: evaluates a wide spectrum of modern LLMs, reasoning models (e.g., o1, o3, DeepSeek-R1, GPT-5), domain-specific models (ChemDFM, ChemLLM, Galactica), and vision-language models on image inputs.

Insightful error analysis and diagnostics: provides concrete findings explaining why current general LLMs struggle with molecular tasks, notably connecting atom localization failures to BPE subword tokenization, and evaluating prompt sensitivity and variance across runs.
weaknesses: Relatively small test set size for generation and editing tasks: the core evaluation set contains 200 samples each for editing and generation (with a 200-sample extended set). While understandable given the heavy human annotation effort, this limits extensive stratification across diverse chemical spaces and rare scaffolds.

Omission of specialized graph-language multimodal baselines: although the paper notes practical graph-language models remain underdeveloped, existing open-source graph-language models (e.g., MolCA, InstructMol) could have been tested on at least a subset of the tasks to provide a more comprehensive multimodal baseline comparison.

Heavy reliance on closed-source proprietary APIs: the primary findings and strongest results are centered around proprietary OpenAI models (e.g., GPT-5, o3, GPT Image 1), which can present reproducibility and long-term versioning challenges for future benchmark comparisons.

strengths: Rigorous, multi-stage human annotation pipeline: The editing and generation tasks are curated through an extensive three-stage verification process (instruction writer, peer reviewer, and two independent chemistry validators reconstructing the structures from scratch), which helps ensure that prompts are deterministic and unambiguous.

Insightful diagnosis of model failure modes: The paper provides compelling qualitative and quantitative analyses of why current models fail, notably demonstrating how BPE tokenization impairs character/atom-level localization, revealing near-random guessing on stereochemical (E/Z) reasoning, and showing that image generation models frequently violate basic chemical valency rules.

Cross-modal evaluation: The benchmark investigates both sequence representations (SMILES) and visual depictions (molecular graphs/images), offering a direct comparison between text LLMs and vision-language multimodal models on identical chemical reasoning tasks.

Thorough sensitivity and variance analyses: The authors demonstrate robustness across prompt variations (including SMILES enumeration variants, chemical terminology substitutions, and non-chemical paraphrasing) and quantify run-to-run variance across API calls.
weaknesses: Limited dataset size for core manual tasks: The core benchmark for molecule editing and generation contains only 200 instances each. While the time-intensive nature of expert validation is understandable, 200 test instances represents a relatively narrow sample of chemical space and limits the statistical granularity when breaking down results across diverse sub-categories of edits.

Incremental novelty in recognition tasks: The 18 molecular structure recognition subtasks (e.g., k-hop neighbors, atom counting, functional group detection) are programmatically generated using standard RDKit scripts over SMILES strings. Similar graph-traversal and substructure extraction tests have been explored in prior chemistry-LLM benchmarks, offering limited novelty.

Heavy reliance on closed-source proprietary APIs: The main benchmark tables exclusively feature frontier closed-source proprietary models (primarily from OpenAI), with only DeepSeek-R1 tested among open/semi-open models. Open-source foundational models (e.g., Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, Mistral) are missing from the primary evaluation, and domain models are relegated to a brief appendix table, limiting reproducibility and accessibility for the broader research community.

Rigid exact-match evaluation for text-to-molecule generation: Relying strictly on exact canonical SMILES / InChIKey matching against ground-truth can unfairly penalize valid generations that strictly satisfy the natural language prompt but differ slightly due to trivial stereochemical defaults, tautomeric forms, or alternative valid interpretations of open-ended phrasing.

Absence of graph-language model baselines: While the introduction frames inherent molecular graphs as an essential modality in chemistry AI workflows, the benchmark does not evaluate any graph-text multimodal models, leaving a gap between the paper's stated motivation and its empirical scope.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and timely problem in AI for chemistry: bridging the gap between natural language and molecular structures via deterministic, unambiguous, and structurally grounded tasks (recognition, editing, and de novo generation).

Exceptionally rigorous data curation pipeline: recognition tasks are programmatically verified via RDKit to ensure determinism, while editing and generation tasks use a multi-step expert human workflow with peer review and dual-blind validator reconstruction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning state-of-the-art frontier models (e.g., GPT-5, o3, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.1, DeepSeek-R1), chemistry-specific LLMs (ChemDFM, ChemLLM), and multimodal approaches (vision-language models and image generation models).

Insightful diagnostic analyses: the paper clearly demonstrates the drop between recognition and localization accuracy, attributes localization errors to BPE tokenization merging atom indices, highlights major stereochemical blind spots, and shows that intermediate structural reasoning aids downstream property prediction.

Well-structured and thorough presentation, with extensive documentation, robust reproducibility reporting (variance analysis, pass@k metrics, prompt sensitivity), and detailed qualitative error categorizations in the appendix.
weaknesses: The dataset size for editing and generation is relatively modest (200 core samples and 200 extended samples per task). While justified by the heavy annotation cost (30–60 minutes per instance with expert chemists), it limits extensive fine-grained stratification across specific chemical reaction classes.

The benchmark is purely evaluative and does not propose a concrete modeling solution, training recipe, or specialized tokenizer to mitigate the identified deficiencies (e.g., character/atom tokenization bottlenecks or stereochemistry representation).

A significant portion of the primary results relies on proprietary, closed-source frontier model APIs whose exact architectures and training corpora are unknown, although snapshot dates are properly documented.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and timely bottleneck in AI for chemistry: bridging the semantic gap between natural language instructions and precise molecular structures, avoiding the ambiguity of previous text-to-molecule benchmarks.

Rigorous data curation and validation pipeline: editing and generation tasks are curated with independent chemist annotations and double-blind validation to ensure deterministic, unambiguous 1:1 mappings.
Broad and up-to-date benchmark evaluation across state-of-the-art reasoning models (e.g., GPT-5, o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, DeepSeek-R1), chemistry-specific LLMs, and multimodal vision-language models.

Insightful mechanistic analysis: identifies key failure modes such as BPE tokenization merging multiple atoms into single tokens (causing localization and enumeration errors) and widespread deficiencies in stereochemical reasoning.

Demonstrates practical downstream relevance: empirically proves that intermediate molecular structure recognition directly improves downstream property prediction (e.g., on MoleculeNet BBBP and BACE benchmarks).
Extensive appendix with thorough robustness checks, including prompt sensitivity analysis, variance across repeated runs, pass@k metrics, and SELFIES representations.
weaknesses: The dataset size for editing and generation is relatively modest (200 core instances each, with 200 extended instances), which limits its utility as a training dataset and primarily confines it to an evaluation benchmark.
The structural descriptions in the generation task are somewhat artificial and stylized compared to how medicinal chemists naturally articulate target compounds in real-world de novo design settings.

The scope is restricted to molecules with fewer than 40 non-hydrogen atoms and focuses predominantly on 2D constitution and stereochemistry, without testing 3D conformational reasoning or macrocyclic systems.

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and timely problem in AI for chemistry: bridging natural language and exact molecular structure via unambiguous, deterministic tasks (recognition, editing, and generation) rather than ambiguous pharmacological descriptions.

Rigorous data curation and verification protocol: combining automated cheminformatics (RDKit) extraction with a multi-stage, dual-expert annotation and independent reconstruction pipeline guarantees high-quality, one-to-one ground-truth mappings.

Comprehensive and up-to-date empirical evaluation covering a wide spectrum of frontier reasoning LLMs, standard LLMs, vision-language models, chemistry-specific models, and multiple molecular representations (SMILES, SELFIES, molecular images, and graphs).

Insightful diagnostic and failure analyses: the paper clearly demonstrates the discrepancy between semantic recognition and precise atom localization (linking it to BPE tokenization issues), highlights stereochemical blindness across models, and shows that articulating molecular structure improves downstream property prediction.
Exemplary reproducibility and robustness analysis, including pass@k metrics, multi-run variance measurements, prompt sensitivity studies, and inclusion of dataset canary strings.
weaknesses: The dataset size for the editing and generation tasks is relatively small (200 core and 200 extended instances per task), which is understandable given the manual annotation cost (30-60 min/instance) but limits the benchmark's utility for model fine-tuning or fine-grained stratification.

The benchmark relies heavily on closed-source commercial APIs (e.g., GPT-5, o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro), which may change or deprecate versions over time, whereas open-source chemical LLMs still struggle significantly with basic task following.

The format of long natural language structural descriptions for de novo generation is somewhat synthetic compared to authentic medicinal chemistry communication (e.g., IUPAC naming or reaction schemes), although it serves well as a controlled test of spatial and compositional reasoning.
